Author_or_Organisation: Deori, C.; Begum, S. S.; Mao, A. A.
Title: Ethnobotany of Sujen—a local rice beer of Deori tribe of Assam
Publication_or_Source_Type: Research article; Indian Journal of Traditional Knowledge 6(1), 121–125
Geographic_Scope: Sunpura Deori gaon (Sadiya, Tinsukia); Kololuwah (Dibrugarh); Rajabari (Sivasagar)
Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Sujen and Mod pitha starter
Claims_Supported: Full text reviewed: 2003–2004 field study in Sunpura Deori gaon, Sadiya (Tinsukia); Kololuwah (Dibrugarh); Rajabari (Sivasagar). Researchers interviewed villagers who regularly prepared Sujen and observed the complete process. Table 1 transcribed to research/assam/sujen-mod-pitha-32-species-src009.csv: 32 listed taxa. Authors say the broad method was similar across the three villages, while plant counts used varied among families; the table does not allocate each taxon to a specific village. Botanical identifications consulted Regional Herbarium Assam and Botanical Survey of India, Eastern Circle. Source-specific method: 3–5 kg rice soaked ~2h; plant materials sun-dried; old Mod pitha used as inoculant; cakes dried above kitchen hearth for a couple of weeks and stored in small earthen pots. Brewing account reports summer fermentation 3–4 days, winter about one week, and historical storage observations.
Limitations_or_Caveats: Historical fieldwork only (2003–2004); not current prevalence. Do not infer that all 32 taxa occur in all three villages or are used by every household. The paper reports 32 species and also says >100 were used 'in olden days'; that historical recollection is not an inventory. Fermentation/storage timings are study observations, not food-safety guidance. Table contains source taxonomic spellings and some inconsistencies; preserve source transcription pending taxonomic review.

Author_or_Organisation: Keot, Jyotshna; Bora, Sudipta Sankar; Kangabam, Rajiv Das; Barooah, Madhumita
Title: Assessment of microbial quality and health risks associated with traditional rice wine starter Xaj-pitha of Assam, India: a step towards defined and controlled fermentation
Publication_or_Source_Type: Research article; 3 Biotech 10, 64; DOI 10.1007/s13205-020-2059-z
Geographic_Scope: Twelve clusters across six Upper Brahmaputra Valley districts: Tinsukia, Dibrugarh, Sivasagar, Jorhat, Lakhimpur and Dhemaji; named clusters include Margherita, Sadiya, Moran, Naharkatiya, Bokota, Sonari, Titabar, Nimati, Bihpuria, Dhakuakhana, Bordoloni and Silapathar
Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Ahom Xaj-pitha starter culture; experimental Xaj fermentation and defined mixed-culture development
Claims_Supported: Full text: 60 Xaj-pitha samples (5 per cluster, 2 clusters in each of 6 districts); 12 cluster composites for culture-based diversity, and one representative Titabar/Jorhat composite for WGS. Reports district/cluster microbial counts, seven-day fermentation dynamics, contaminants, 22 mould strains (13 amylase-positive; four selected), eight yeast isolates, strain-level safety/functionality screening and a candidate defined consortium of Amylomyces rouxii ABT82, Saccharomycopsis fibuligera ADJ4 and Saccharomyces cerevisiae ABT-Y1J. Full audit: research/assam/src024-keot-2020-xaj-pitha-fulltext-audit-2026-11-04.md.
Limitations_or_Caveats: Not a statewide or cross-community survey. One composite, not all 60 samples, underwent metagenomic sequencing. The Titabar WGS component reuses the same underlying dataset reported in SRC-023 (Bora et al. 2016): same MG-RAST identifier and distinctive sequence totals; count as one shared WGS dataset, not independent replication. The 60-sample culture-based survey and 12 cluster composites remain additional separate evidence. Exact sample-code crosswalk is not published. See research/assam/src023-src024-xaj-pitha-metagenome-dataset-reuse-audit-2026-11-04.md. Culture counts and organism detection are starter-specific; not proof of all taxa in finished beverage or universal consumer risk. Two yeast strains showed biogenic-amine production ability; all tested mould cultures were negative for aflatoxin only, not all mycotoxins. Candidate defined consortium is experimental, not shown to be household-adopted or a universal validated safe starter. No sample-to-household identities or full producer-level process records.

Author_or_Organisation: Das, R.; Medhi, M. C.; Tamang, B.
Title: Microbial diversity and its links to retinol pathways and aroma compounds in ethnic fermented rice beverages of Assam
Publication_or_Source_Type: Peer-reviewed research article, AMB Express 16, article 91
Geographic_Scope: Pukia, Dhemaji district (Black Rohi Modh BR and Rohi Modh RH); Kaljar, Baksa district (Jou Bidwi JOU); Jamuuri Panchali, Dhemaji district (Sai Mod SM); sample coordinates referenced in Supplementary File ST1
Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Black Rohi Modh; Rohi Modh; Jou Bidwi; Sai Mod; household batch-level microbiome, physicochemical and metabolomic comparisons
Claims_Supported: Full text documents 12 sample units representing four beverages, but explicitly states each beverage was collected once as one authentic household batch; triplicates are technical, not independent biological replicates. BR and RH both sampled in Pukia, Dhemaji; JOU in Kaljar, Baksa; SM in Jamuuri Panchali, Dhemaji. The paper reports black-rice BR and common-rice RH separately, HPLC ethanol, DPPH/FRAP, microbial isolates, metagenomic profiles and GC-MS/MS metabolomics. Supplement ST1 contains sample codes and GPS coordinates; main-text map identifies Pukia for BR and RH. The article's Data Availability statement deposits raw shotgun-metagenomic data under NCBI BioProject PRJNA1284041; Sanger sequence accessions are provided with organism/yeast labels in Fig. 3. A structured summary of aggregate microbiome/metabolome metrics is stored in `research/assam/src046-microbiome-metabolome-summary.csv`.
Limitations_or_Caveats: The source labels the producer community broadly as Kachari; exact subcommunity and household identities are not established in the accessible main text. BR is one household batch and may be a black-rice variant of Rohi rather than a distinct locally named tradition. No sample-specific starter recipe or complete fermentation sequence for BR is provided; the article's general Rohi Modh account mentions Bora chaul and aaroi. Technical replicates do not provide biological replication; statistics and correlations are exploratory with n=4 independent product batches. HPLC and GC-MS/MS ethanol estimates differ and must remain separate. Antioxidant assays are in-vitro and not clinical health evidence. Retinol pathway annotations indicate predicted microbial metabolic potential, not direct vitamin A production. Supplementary GPS and detailed ST2-ST5 data require separate extraction; the DOCX link was not accessible in this pass. Supplementary File ST1 (sample GPS) and ST2–ST5 (proximate, isolate, metataxonomy and metabolomics data) are referenced by the publisher, but the DOCX was not retrieved in this pass. Raw shotgun metagenomic reads are separately cited by the article under BioProject PRJNA1284041; that accession has not yet been expanded into individual SRA run/sample records. 2026-11-07 recheck: full article text directly confirms the JOU sample locality Kaljar, Baksa and SM sample locality Jamuuri Panchali, Dhemaji; both are single-household batch samples. Place rows ASM-PL-117/118 preserve these source-reported collection sites without asserting village-wide or current production.

Claims_Supported: Full text reviewed (published 21 June 2026; DOI 10.32859/era.34.75.1-31): field survey in ten named Mising-dominant Jorhat villages (Charighoria, Upor Kareng, Kalbari, Neulgaon, Bormukoli, Bahfalla, Borpomua gaon, Kumarbari gaon, Jengrai Chapori, Kawoimari Bonoria Mishing Gaon), visited monthly for 12 consecutive months during March 2024–2025; 50 informants (17 men, 33 women). Limitations_or_Caveats: Study villages are field sites, not ten confirmed production sites for both drinks. Reported medicinal/nutritional benefits are not clinical evidence.

Title: Exploring the microbiota and metabolites of traditional rice beer varieties of Assam and their functionalities
Publication_or_Source_Type: Peer-reviewed research article; 3 Biotech 9:174
Geographic_Scope: Nine villages in Assam; Mising sample codes RB01 (Poro Apong), RB02 and RB03 (Nogin Apong); village-to-code mapping is in supplementary Table S1, not publicly retrievable in current review
Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Mising Poro Apong and Nogin Apong; Ahom Xaaj; Bodo Joubishi
Claims_Supported: Reports 27 finished-beverage samples from nine villages; triplicate samples from each location were pooled equally into nine composite samples. Mising codes: RB01=Poro Apong; RB02/RB03=Nogin Apong. 16S rDNA sequences deposited under MG-RAST study mgp85043. Supplementary Table S1 carries village/sample mapping; Table S2 rice varieties and starter herbs. See research/assam/apong-microbiology-crosswalk-2026-11-09.md.
Limitations_or_Caveats: The accessible PMC record marks the supplementary DOCX as available to authorized users; S1 and S2 were not retrieved. Do not infer village names or map RB01/RB02/RB03 to known Apong localities. Each code is a pooled location composite, not a single household batch. 16S rDNA describes bacterial DNA in finished beverages, not starter-cake yeasts/moulds; DNA detection does not establish viability. MG-RAST study identifier is cited in article but sample-level metadata was not independently retrieved.

Author_or_Organisation: Mili, Chiranjib; Lagachu, Manab Jyoti; Basumatary, Jwngma; Tayung, Kumananda
Title: Decoding the flavour chemistry of PO:RO APONG, a traditional rice beer of Northeast India
Publication_or_Source_Type: Review article; Food Research International: Reports 1, article 100006; online publication listed in 2026

Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: PO:RO APONG flavour chemistry; OPOB/Epop starter-plant phytochemicals; fermentative microbes; ash-mediated chemistry
Claims_Supported: Synthesizes prior research on interactions among starter-culture plant phytochemicals, fermentative microbes and rice-straw/husk ash; discusses Maillard reactions and potential effects on colour and flavour. Identifies gaps in mechanisms and reproducibility.
Limitations_or_Caveats: Secondary review, not a new village-level field study or standalone validation of individual mechanisms. Full text was not accessible in this review; claims should be cross-checked against cited primary studies. Do not treat flavour/chemical discussion as evidence of clinical benefit or safety.

Author_or_Organisation: Pegu, Rajeswar; Gogoi, Jitu; Tamuli, Ajit K.; Teron, Robindra
Title: Apong, an alcoholic beverage of cultural significance of the Mising community of Northeast India
Publication_or_Source_Type: Peer-reviewed research article; Global Journal of Interdisciplinary Social Sciences 2(6):12–17
Geographic_Scope: Mising communities in Dhemaji district and Majuli Island, Assam, and Mising communities in Pasighat and Oyan, East Siang district, Arunachal Pradesh; study fieldwork in 2010 and 2012
Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Nogin Apong; Po:ro Apong (saimod); E’pob starter; Ta:suk extraction; cultural and ethnobotanical knowledge
Claims_Supported: Documents traditional knowledge using discussions, semi-structured interviews and personal observations. Distinguishes Nogin Apong (fermented rice with E’pob) from Po:ro Apong (rice, usually glutinous, with ash of paddy husk and straw). Limitations_or_Caveats: Fieldwork is dated 2010 and 2012 and should be treated as historical, source-specific documentation. Reported community beliefs about health effects are not clinical evidence. Do not interpret filtration as distillation or assume this process is universal across all Mising localities.

Author_or_Organisation: Talukdar, Simi; Jyethi, Darpa Saurav; Sarma, Barasa; Talukdar, Homen
Title: Cultural ecology and conservation of traditional beverage practices among selected communities of Assam, Northeast India
Publication_or_Source_Type: Peer-reviewed open-access research article; Discover Food 6:376
Geographic_Scope: Fieldwork in Kokrajhar and Baksa (Bodo), Goalpara and Kamrup (Rabha), and Tinsukia and Dibrugarh (Ahom), Assam; fieldwork reported for February 2023–2024
Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Bodo, Rabha and Ahom traditional fermented beverages; beverage-associated plants, cultural practices and knowledge transmission
Claims_Supported: Reports 30 informants (10 per community), 41 plant species across 29 families, and 85% wild-sourced; methods include semi-structured interviews, focus groups, participant observation and plant collection/identification. Publisher metadata lists Published 23 June 2026 and Version of Record 4 September 2026. Methods state herbarium specimens were deposited at Arunachal University of Studies.
Limitations_or_Caveats: Study-site districts are not a production census and do not establish village-level beverage attribution. Table 1 attributes plants to communities but has no beverage-specific column. Audit of archived transcription: 41 rows and 41 distinct scientific-name strings; community labels occur on 35 Ahom, 20 Bodo and 16 Rabha rows; only 8 rows are labelled for all three communities although the narrative says 24/41. Narrative life-form counts sum to 47 against 41 species; table-row labels count 13 herbs, 10 shrubs, 9 trees, 4 climbers, 3 ferns, 1 small tree and 1 woody climber. Methods describe FL as percentage x100 but reported values are mostly around 1–4; scale/formula needs clarification. Preserve source values; do not silently correct. Table 1 prints ST/EES/2024/015 for two taxa; verify against herbarium records. Community-reported medicinal uses are not clinical evidence, and conservation effects are not established causally by the qualitative design. See research/assam/cross-community-2026-source-quality-audit.md and research/assam/src-091-voucher-audit.md.

Author_or_Organisation: Barman, P.; Roy, K.; Sahu, R.

Author_or_Organisation: Das, Utpala; Rabha, David; Das, Jugabrat

Author_or_Organisation: Das, A. J.; Khawas, P.; Miyaji, T.; Deka, S. C.

Claims_Supported: Open-access full text reports nine samples across four states; triplicate laboratory measurements of alcohol, pH, organic acids, carbohydrates, amino acids and volatile/aromatic compounds. Limitations_or_Caveats: Historic small sample set: one sample code per named Assam beverage/locality; analytical triplicates are not independent household replicates. Values are sample-specific, not standard product specifications, current prevalence evidence or safety guidance. The paper’s broad health/safety conclusions are not accepted as clinical evidence. Preserve the source’s spellings (Sibsagar/Xaj-pani) and distinguish sample locality from village-level production. See research/assam/src-105-biochemical-sample-audit.md.

Title: HRLC-MS analysis of Apong starter culture (E’pob): The starter cake used for the preparation of traditional rice beer of the Mising tribe of Assam

Author_or_Organisation: Yumnam, Hanna; Hazarika, Parijat; Sharma, Indu
Title: Metagenomic insights into traditional fermentation of rice-based beverages among ethnic tribes in southern Assam, Northeast India
Publication_or_Source_Type: Original research article; Frontiers in Microbiology 15:1410098
Geographic_Scope: Southern Assam; five community cohorts; exact sample villages and sample-specific districts not reported in accessible main text
Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Zeme Naga Zao/Zou; Dimasa Kachari Judima; Hmar Zu; Karbi Hor Alank; Tea-tribe Haria
Claims_Supported: Fifteen traditionally prepared, non-commercial pre-distillation beverage samples (three per community cohort) are stated in the article. The study used Illumina MiSeq bacterial 16S rRNA V3–V4 amplicon sequencing. NCBI BioProject PRJNA1017140 resolves to SRA Study SRP460503, five BioSamples and five experiments/runs (one per cohort: SRR26058871–SRR26058875); sample names TT, DMK, ZN, K1, HM. BioSample records give dates from 2022-06-21 to 2022-07-25, but only geographic location 'India' and the same repeated coordinate pair 20.59 N, 78.96 E for all five; they also link to PRJNA994679.
Limitations_or_Caveats: Despite title/terminology, method is targeted bacterial 16S V3–V4 amplicon sequencing, not untargeted shotgun metagenomics; no fungal ITS profiling. Major unresolved discrepancy: paper states 15 collected samples (3/cohort), while NCBI lists only 5 BioSamples and 5 SRA runs (one/cohort); pooling vs incomplete deposition is not established. BioSample geography is not locality-grade: all five repeat 20.59 N, 78.96 E and say only India; do not use as southern Assam sample coordinates. Each BioSample also links to PRJNA994679, relationship unverified. Exact villages, producer households and sample-to-village mapping not disclosed. Cohort tables aggregate results. No beverage-specific taxon abundance values transcribed from plotted figure. PICRUSt outputs are inferred functions, not measured genes/metabolites. Article contains inconsistent Zao/Zou spelling and statistical-text inconsistency: unweighted UniFrac sentence reports p>0.05 while calling it significant; PERMANOVA phylum-level p=0.2 is not significant. Do not make health/probiotic/safety claims. A second BioProject (PRJNA994679) is linked from each of the five BioSamples; its title/description refer to shotgun metagenomics of fermented rice products from southern Assam and its project page lists 10 experiments/6 BioSamples, but it also links an apparently unrelated yak gut virome publication. Relationship to SRC-132 and overlap with its samples remain unresolved; do not merge or treat as evidence that the 2024 article performed shotgun sequencing.

Author_or_Organisation: Kardong, D.; Deori, K.; Sood, K.; Yadav, R. N. S.; Bora, T. C.; Gogoi, B. K.
Title: Evaluation of Nutritional and Biochemical aspects of Po:ro apong (Saimod) — A home made alcoholic rice beverage of Mising tribe of Assam, India
Publication_or_Source_Type: Primary biochemical and process study; Indian Journal of Traditional Knowledge 11(3):499–504
Geographic_Scope: Mising households, Dibrugarh district, Upper Assam
Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Po:ro Apong / Saimod; Epop starter
Claims_Supported: Full text retrieved and audited. Describes Epop starter preparation, 100 g powdered Epop per 3 kg cooked rice, rice-husk/rice-straw ash, fermentation for about 20 days at 30–35°C, ripe mash called Po:ro arouk, and extraction through bamboo Ta:suk filtration with warm water. Traditional sensory markers: mild fruity-sweet aroma by days 2–3 and strong fruity/pungent odour around days 8–10. Author_or_Organisation: Borkotoky, Babita Phukan; Neog, Mridula; Barua, Iswar Chandra
Title: Mishing’s Apong – An Intangible Cultural Heritage of Assam
Publication_or_Source_Type: Research article reproduced in The Exalted Edition / IJHEPS, Issue 7, digital pp. 59–63; ISSN 2320-2955
Geographic_Scope: Mising-dominated areas of Jorhat district, Assam; five named villages: Sirum, Budubari, Boloma, Bhomoraguri and Arunamukh
Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Nogin Apong; Po:ro Apong / Saimod; Epop / Epoppitha starter culture
Claims_Supported: Full article text retrieved in digital issue. Repeated survey in Jorhat; prepared starter and beverages collected mostly from five named villages; plant collection April–June 2011 and 2012; voucher specimens reportedly deposited in Kakojan College Herbarium after identification with AAU Jorhat Weed Herbarium and BSI Eastern Circle, Shillong. Authors claim 51 plant species in 39 genera and 31 families, but the Table 1 plant inventory is not reliably exposed in the accessible text layer and no plant rows have been transcribed. Starter method: plant parts sun-dried 2–3 days, ground, mixed with soaked rice and old Epop, cakes 2–5 cm, incubated about 3 days on bamboo frame 1.5 m above kitchen fire and sun-dried 2–3 days; claimed storage about two months. Nogin: tightly cooked rice, 4–8 Epop/kg, 3–4 days in pots. Po:ro: specially burnt rice-husk/hay ash mixed with cooked rice before starter until rice blackens; pot fermentation 15–20 days; water percolation through banana-leaf-lined conical bamboo frame; filtrate collected in earthen pots. Microbiology: three Saccharomyces species and one each Mucor and Rhizopus reported from starter culture; authors report no Enterobacteriaceae or lactic-acid bacteria growth on their selected culture media. Reported viable yeast/mould count 118 × 10^7 per ml original culture sample. Article reports 5% alcohol in both Apong varieties; Nogin higher carbohydrate, protein, fat and calorific value than Po:ro; about 11 free amino acids reported in both.
Limitations_or_Caveats: Digital magazine/flipbook reproduction rather than a publisher-hosted journal archive; publication year is unresolved because the masthead says January 2014 while page 2 says January 2015, FlipHTML5 records publication on 17 January 2015, and the Kakojan College author profile lists it in 2015. Use 2014 as the printed issue year; retain the institutional 2015 profile discrepancy. The article’s Table 1 is not reliably available as text; do not invent or transcribe 51 plant names from secondary snippets. The authors describe extensive/repeated survey but give no informant or household count and no village-by-village allocation. Five villages are stated as the main collection sites; do not imply all 51 taxa occur at each village. Voucher deposition is stated but no accession numbers are supplied. Microbial identification is only to the group or lowest possible genera in methods; reported organism counts are not equivalent to modern molecular species identification. Negative culture results apply only to the media/incubation conditions used. Biochemical results are source-specific; no health benefit or food-safety inference is justified. The 5% alcohol value is not a universal specification and differs from other Po:ro studies.

Author_or_Organisation: Kardong, Devid; Pegu, Bhaba Kr.; Ghose Guha, Bijeta
Title: Evaluation of Efficacy of the Microbial Consortium for Fermentation of Alcoholic Rice Beverage amongst Mising Tribe of Assam, India
Publication_or_Source_Type: Primary experimental study; Current Trends in Pharmaceutical Research 4(2); Article 21; Dibrugarh University-hosted PDF
Geographic_Scope: Mising household starter culture collected from unspecified localities in Mising-populated areas; no village-level sample mapping
Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Po:ro Apong / Saimod; traditional home-made starter (HMS) versus laboratory-made starter (LMS) and microbial consortium
Claims_Supported: Compares fermentation mash after 144 hours. HMS uses traditional household starter; laboratory consortium comprised two amylolytic fungi (Mucor sp. and Saccharomycopsis sp.) plus one Saccharomyces sp. yeast isolated from HMS. After 144 h HMS mash: pH 4.78; reducing sugar 17 ± 0.12 mg/g; titratable acidity 0.22 ± 0.01% lactic acid; ethanol 3.1 ± 0.02 ml/100 g mash. LMSP and MC produced lower ethanol/acidity and higher final bacterial colony counts. Table 3 includes starting/final microbial load and all comparator values; see research/assam/apong-microbiology-crosswalk-2026-11-09.md.
Limitations_or_Caveats: Experimental preliminary study with limited reporting: no named villages, household count, biological replicate design or detailed temperature/time-course series. The 144-hour endpoint is six days, not the full household maturation period described in SRC-136. HMS and laboratory formulations differ in microbial diversity and substrate preparation, so result does not isolate the causal contribution of individual plant ingredients. Paper inconsistently describes 14 herbs in results although abstract says 13 herb ingredients. Do not generalize this single laboratory comparison to all Mising households or recipes.

Author_or_Organisation: Pegu, Bhaba Kumar; Sarmah, Puja; Yein, Jelshing; Sanong, James

Author_or_Organisation: Pawe, Dimbo; Gogoi, Rajib
Title: Ethnobotany of Poro Apong or Chai Mod — A local rice beer of Mishing tribes of Assam
Publication_or_Source_Type: Primary ethnobotanical article; NeBIO: An International Journal of Environment and Biodiversity 4(2):46–49; full text readable on ResearchGate
Geographic_Scope: Mishing-dominated localities in Lakhimpur and Sonitpur districts, Assam; seven selected villages named: Dhunaguri, Badati, Bongalmora, Chamaguri Temona, Luitmukh, Kathalkuchi and Rajbari
Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Poro Apong / Chai Mod; comparative mention of Nogin Apong; Poro-specific Apob starter culture
Claims_Supported: Full text recovered. Authors report interviews with villagers who regularly prepare Poro and direct observation of the complete method; plant collections identified with confirmation at BSI Shillong herbarium (ASSAM) and Itanagar (ARUN). Table 1 explicitly lists 28 plant taxa for Poro Apob: 27 visible serials, with two Thelypteris names in row 25 and serial 26 absent. Inventory: research/assam/src170-pawe-gogoi-2013-poro-apob-28-taxon-inventory.csv. Source-specific process: 2–4 kg rice soaked 2–3 h for Apob; cakes dried above kitchen fireplace 3–5 days; Poro mash includes straw/rice-husk ash and 4–5 crushed Apob cakes; fermentation 7–12 days by season (sometimes over a month), then water filtration/re-filtration through banana-leaf/straw-lined Tasuk until brown.
Limitations_or_Caveats: No field dates, informant count, voucher accession numbers or plant-by-village matrix. Table numbering skips 26; the two taxa in row 25 explain the reported 28 species if counted separately, but the article does not explain the numbering gap. The article's traditional medicinal claims are not clinical or safety evidence. The recovered method describes filtration through Tasuk, not distillation; do not generalize across households or reconcile conflicting accounts by inference. Full audit: research/assam/src170-pawe-gogoi-2013-poro-apong-acquisition-audit.md.
